tagline.text: Islands with the clearest water between El Nido and Coron

items.credit: Paul Christian B. Yang-ed / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: More than 50 islands scattered in the sea between El Nido and Coron, known for water so clear that a foreign travel outlet once ranked it at the top of its list of "seas to swim in before you die." Tourist facilities are almost nonexistent, but it's Palawan's last frontier, where you can have uninhabited beaches, coral reefs, and island camping all to yourself.

Linapacan is an island municipality at the southern end of the Calamian group, between Culion Island and the northern tip of mainland Palawan. Its administrative center is San Miguel on Linapacan Island, and more than 50 islands large and small are scattered here, including 10 with their own barangays. The population is about 17,000, most of whom make their living through fishing, seaweed farming, and cashew growing.
It split off from Coron in

to become its own municipality, but to this day no airport or regular fast craft serves it, so tourism development has barely happened. As a result, most of the islands remain uninhabited, and the coral reefs and white sand beaches have seen little human impact. When a foreign travel outlet placed Linapacan at the top of its list of "seas to swim in before you die," the island became known for having some of the clearest water in the Philippines.

On calm days, you can clearly see the sandy bottom and coral several meters down, right from the boat. Traveling between islands by bangka, stepping onto nameless beaches to snorkel, buying fish from fishing villages to grill and eat, and stargazing under a sky with no light pollution at night — that's the whole appeal of traveling here.

Electricity, communication, lodging, and restaurants are all limited, and boat schedules are irregular, so this isn't a comfortable resort destination. It's recommended for travelers who've already visited El Nido and Coron, want a quiet sea instead of crowded tours, or are adventurous types who enjoy camping and a bit of inconvenience. You can also pass through as part of an expedition-style boat trip between El Nido and Coron.
The core of a Linapacan trip. Just floating offshore from a beach, you can clearly see tropical fish and starfish moving among the coral, as vivid as an aquarium.
Charter a bangka for a day and visit three or four empty white sand beaches. Having a beach entirely to yourself for a whole day is hard to experience in El Nido or Coron.
A well-preserved reef off this island, considered a top snorkeling spot. A camp charging a beach fee is here, making it a good place to stop for lunch and rest.
Shallow coral gardens spread around this small island, which travelers often rate as the best spot for snorkeling in Linapacan.
A few islands have simple camps with tents and cabins. Sleeping to the sound of waves and walking an empty beach at sunrise makes for a night you'll remember for a long time.
In island villages like San Miguel, Nangalao, and Kalibangbangan, you can watch residents drying seaweed and mending nets up close.

blocks.title: A sky with no light pollution

children.text: On many islands, electricity runs for only a few hours in the evening, so the sky turns pitch dark at night. On clear dry-season nights, the Milky Way is vividly visible.
Taking an expedition-style boat trip between El Nido and Coron, sailing over 3–5 days and staying at island camps, is a comfortable way to see Linapacan's islands.

Boat schedules change often depending on weather and day of the week, so it's safer to add a spare day at the end of your trip and fly out from El Nido or Coron.
Linapacan has no airport. Since
March 29, 2026
, direct flights from Manila to Busuanga and El Nido have ended, so you either fly from Clark to Busuanga Airport (USU) in about
1 hour 20 minutes
and take a boat from Coron, or fly from Clark to El Nido Airport (ENI) in about
1 hour 35 minutes
and take a boat from the El Nido side. There are also direct flights to both airports from Cebu.

Some of the large passenger bangkas running between Coron and El Nido stop at Linapacan, taking about
3–4 hours
from either Coron or El Nido. Fares run around

From San Fernando, an east-coast town about
1 hour

The fast craft between Coron and El Nido only passes offshore from Linapacan without stopping. All boat services can be cancelled at any time due to weather, so check the latest schedule information.
Chartering a bangka in Coron or San Fernando costs about
per boat one way, varying with boat size and passenger count. You can add island hopping along the way, making this the most practical option if you're traveling with a group.
All inter-island travel is by bangka. Arranging a full-day charter through your lodging or a fisherman costs about
per boat, varying with fuel prices. Within San Miguel island, you can walk or rent a motorbike.

to

is the dry season, and the best time is
March–May
, when the winds die down. During this period, the sea is often mirror-calm, giving the clearest water, and it's easy to travel between islands even by small bangka. During
December–February
, the northeast Amihan wind blows, and the Coron–Linapacan stretch can see high waves on some days, occasionally cancelling sailings.
June
to
October

brings the southwest Habagat monsoon, with frequent rain and waves, and the water often turns murky. When a typhoon passes through, boats can be grounded for days, potentially stranding you on the island, so a visit during this period isn't recommended. Midday temperatures run around
year-round, and sun exposure is very strong on islands with little shade.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
There are two types of lodging. San Miguel, the administrative center, has a few simple lodges and homestays at about
a night, while a few islands have camps renting out tents or bamboo cabins at about

a night. Most can't be booked online and require a phone call or Facebook message, and with only a handful of rooms, you may find nowhere to stay if you don't check ahead. Electricity, from generators or solar power, often runs only in the evening.

Restaurants amount to a few small eateries and sari-sari stores in San Miguel. At camps and homestays, the owner often cooks meals or lends you their kitchen, so buying fish, squid, and crab that fishermen caught that day and asking them to grill it is the tastiest and cheapest way to eat. Rice, vegetables, fruit, snacks, and drinks are hard to find on the island, so it's best to stock up in Coron or El Nido. Cashew nuts and dried fish from this area make simple souvenirs.
Assume there's no ATM in Linapacan, and bring all the cash you'll need — including boat charter and lodging costs — from Coron or El Nido.
A power bank and a foldable solar charger come in handy. Many islands only have electricity for a few hours in the evening.
Snorkel gear, aqua shoes, and a waterproof bag are hard to rent locally, so it's best to bring your own.
For boat information, your local lodging or the shipping line's contact is more reliable than the internet. Reconfirm the day before departure whether the boat is running.
Cell signal is generally available near villages but cuts out between islands, so it's best to save offline maps and your lodging's contact info.
Traveling alone drives up costs significantly, so it's more economical to gather a group in Coron or El Nido and share a boat.
If you insert 2–3 days into a trip going from El Nido to Coron, you can visit Linapacan without backtracking.

Linapacan is a remote island area with almost no hospitals or pharmacies, and boats can stop running for days if the weather turns bad. Bring basic medicine, build spare days into your itinerary, and check the latest notices from the coast guard and shipping lines before you leave.
Small bangkas sometimes don't have enough life jackets, so check before departure that there's one for everyone, and always wear it.
Uninhabited-island beaches have no shade, making sunburn and dehydration easy. Bring a hat, a rash guard, and plenty of water.
Don't step on or touch the coral, use reef-safe sunscreen, and take all your trash back out with you.
Some beaches and islands are private property or camp areas that charge a fee. It's best to check with your boatman before stepping ashore.
Night swimming and snorkeling alone are dangerous due to currents, so avoid them.
In
November 2025

, Typhoon Tino (Kalmaegi) passed off the coast of Linapacan, and the island villages suffered heavy damage. Some accommodations, camps, and passenger bangkas may still be under repair or have stopped operating, so contact them directly before departure to confirm they're open.
